openingMessage: The price of success is hard work, dedication to the job at hand, and the determination that whether we win or lose, we have applied the best of ourselves to the task.
openingWhy: Some days the well wins anyway — weather, downhole, plain luck. What can't ever happen is the well winning because we showed up loose. Rained out and rescheduled with the standard intact is a good day. Finished early with steps skipped is a loss, whatever the ticket says.
leadershipThought: Recognition is culture in action. When you name what someone did right, you tell the whole crew what right looks like. Kudos to the ones doing it right every day.

Stop Work Authority Exercised — Unsafe Man Basket Operations (Line of Fire)
Man basket work is one of the highest-risk lift operations on an oil and gas site — Stop Work Authority before elevation is always the right call when anything about the setup looks wrong.

Positive Observation — LOTO Disconnect Completed Efficiently (Energy Isolation)
LOTO, atmospheric testing, and hold points together form a complete energy control system — don't shortcut any one of them, even on a quick job.

Stop Work by Equipment Operator — Spotter Lost Visual (Mobile Equipment)
Equipment operators own Stop Work Authority too — stop the moment you lose your spotter; regaining visual contact is the only acceptable restart condition.

Crane Work — Horse Head Installation and Flowline Connection (Mobile Equipment)
Crane work demands real-time stop work authority — if anything changes during the lift, the person on the ground is empowered to call the stop immediately.

specialFocus.title: Who Are We? — The Promise We Make Each Other
specialFocus.why:
This one comes from the top, and it's personal. Today I — Mike Lyons — took a call from a company man. Not about our monitors. Not about our paperwork. About camaraderie: he thought there should be more of it among our team. I'm not passing that call down as blame. I'm owning my piece of it, and I'm asking each of us to own ours. Who are we? We are the first ones on location and the last ones to leave. We are AGT and safety oversight — the second set of eyes that ops counts on. And here's the truth about that job: nobody can assign it to you. Walking over when your task is done and asking a teammate if they need a hand isn't a policy — it's a choice each of us makes, alone, every shift, usually when nobody's watching. I want people around me who have my back the way a SEAL team has each other's: you would never not cover your brother. You have his six.

And this is not a weird ask — answer it honestly: what kind of partner do you want supporting you in times of duty? The first name that comes to your mind — that part is easy. Then notice how fast the list drops off after it. Here's the part that belongs to you alone: nobody can put you on someone else's first-name list. You earn your way onto it — one “what can I do?” at a time. That is the promise I'm making to every one of you, and the one I'm asking you to make back: be the one who can be counted on. A crew that makes that promise to each other is a crew nothing gets through.
standard: When my task is done, I am not done. I find my teammates on location and say it out loud: “I'm here to help — what can I do?” Every location, every time.

I stay out of the truck — clear-minded, eyes up, involved. First to location and last to leave means I'm present the whole way through. Ops counts on me as their second set of eyes, and I can't be that from the cab.
I cover my teammate's six. If one of us is still working, I'm still working. Nobody wearing Canon works alone while I stand and watch.
specialFocus.scenario: Two Canon techs on the same pad. One finishes his monitor setup, checks his box, and walks back to the truck. Fifty yards away, his teammate is still setting up alone in the heat. The company man sees all of it — and what he sees isn't laziness. It's two individuals wearing the same logo instead of one team. Now run it the other way: the first tech finishes, walks over, and says 'I'm done — what do you need?' Same two people, same job. But now the work goes faster, the location is safer because there's a second set of eyes on the task, and what the client remembers is a crew that covers each other. Nobody ordered that tech to walk over. That's the whole point — it was his choice, and it changed what Canon looks like to everyone on that pad. We got the other kind of phone call today. Whether there's ever a second one is a choice each of us makes tomorrow morning.
questions: What kind of partner do you want supporting you in times of duty? A name came to mind instantly — why that name? What are they doing that you're not? And the harder question: whose first-name list are YOU on?
When your part of the job is done, what is the very next thing you do — honestly? Do you walk toward your teammate, or toward your truck?
What does having someone's six actually look like on a location? Give me a real example from this week — who covered you, or who did you cover?
If a company man watched only you for an entire shift, would he describe you as 'here to help' or 'here to do a task'? What exactly would he see?
specialFocus.nonNegotiable: My promise: First to location. Last to leave. Out of the truck and involved. Before I head for the gate, I ask every teammate still working: 'What can I do?' I don't leave a brother or sister working alone — I have their six. That is who I am. That is who we are.
